+## Executor scope can change when a call returns
+
+Trace who creates, borrows and closes each executor, and whether work may outlive the submitting
+call. Introducing per-call ownership changes behavior independently of the thread factory.
+The Java 21 `ExecutorService.close()` contract waits for actual task termination; a timeout or
+cancelled Future does not establish that termination.
+
+```java
+// Partial Java 21+ counterexample; requires java.util.concurrent imports.
+// This does not return the Future to its caller while the submitted task is still running.
+static <T> Future<T> start(Callable<T> task) {
+    try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
+        return executor.submit(task);
+    } // close runs before the method returns
+}
+```
+
+Similarly, `Future.get(timeout, unit)` limits that wait, not the following executor close.
+Interruption during close requests cancellation but still waits for executing tasks to finish;
+an interrupt-insensitive operation can keep the caller waiting. Distinguish the response deadline
+from cleanup completion instead of promising both from a timed `get`.
+
+Keep lexical ownership when completion before scope exit is required and its waiting contract
+fits. If tasks may outlive the call, retain or establish an appropriate component/framework owner
+that tracks completion and drains at shutdown; do not close a borrowed executor in the request.
+Preserve admission limits and error observation. Simply omitting shutdown, abandoning tasks or
+releasing their resource permits on Future cancellation does not repair the lifecycle.
+
+Use controlled task completion to check the required return boundary: hold a task open, observe
+the method's return or timeout handling, then allow cleanup to finish. Include cancellation that
+has been requested while the task remains active. A test that only checks the Future's status
+misses a caller still blocked in close.
+

files.CONTRACT.md:
# Launcher contract

The project targets standard Java 21, with no preview features or third-party dependencies. Launcher is an application component retained across calls and closed by its existing outer lifecycle owner. Smoke.java shows that owner. Admission is already bounded before launch; there is no required ordering between submitted tasks, and callers observe failures through their returned Future. Preserve these scope assumptions rather than building a service-wide migration framework.

Launcher.close() must leave no work accepted by this component still executing when it returns. Some tasks cooperate with interruption; others can remain active until a dependency explicitly releases them. The component lifecycle owner can wait for cleanup at shutdown. Do not discard accepted work, suppress its failures, or claim that Future cancellation alone proves cleanup has completed. Public API compatibility and the Java 21 baseline should be preserved where practical; focused internal changes are allowed when the return contract requires them.

## Return boundary

launch must return its Future without waiting for the submitted task to finish. The task is allowed to remain active after launch returns, under the component's lifecycle owner. A caller must be able to obtain the handle while work is still blocked.

# Launcher contract

The project targets standard Java 21, with no preview features or third-party dependencies. Launcher is an application component retained across calls and closed by its existing outer lifecycle owner. Smoke.java shows that owner. Admission is already bounded before launch; there is no required ordering between submitted tasks, and callers observe failures through their returned Future. Preserve these scope assumptions rather than building a service-wide migration framework.

Launcher.close() must leave no work accepted by this component still executing when it returns. Some tasks cooperate with interruption; others can remain active until a dependency explicitly releases them. The component lifecycle owner can wait for cleanup at shutdown. Do not discard accepted work, suppress its failures, or claim that Future cancellation alone proves cleanup has completed. Public API compatibility and the Java 21 baseline should be preserved where practical; focused internal changes are allowed when the return contract requires them.

## Return boundary

launch must not return until its submitted task has finished executing. The returned Future may already be completed. Work must not escape this call's execution scope, and no prompt-return deadline is promised while the task remains active.

expectedOutcomes: Identify that the implicit close executes before the return reaches the caller, preventing handle delivery while the task is still running.
Attribute the regression to the new per-call ownership boundary, not a general inability of virtual threads to execute asynchronously.
Implement a proportionate lifecycle solution using the existing component close contract or an equivalently justified owner, keeping the public launch/close API where practical.
Ensure the returned Future can be observed while a controlled task remains active.
Ensure component close/drain does not return while its accepted controlled task remains active, including after Future cancellation.
Preserve Java 21, bounded-admission assumptions, failure observation and orderly shutdown; no dependency/preview upgrade or abandoned daemon task.
Report compiler target separately from runtime and use bounded coordinated checks instead of inferring correctness from a fast smoke task.
controlledChecks: Hold a Callable on a release latch after it signals entry.
Invoke launch on a helper thread so a broken implementation cannot freeze the evaluator.
With the task held open, require launch to deliver a Future; use a bounded test guard, not a throughput claim.
Request Future.cancel(true) while a test callable deliberately remains active until a separate release signal.
Invoke component close on an owned helper; it must wait for actual task completion.
Release task, then join all helpers and observe cleanup/error/interrupt outcomes; keep a finite watchdog.
observableFailures: Leaves per-call try-with-resources unchanged and claims returning Future makes it asynchronous.
Only increases get timeout, changes virtual thread naming/pinning flags, or replaces virtual threads without addressing ownership.
Removes close entirely or detaches task execution with no lifecycle owner/drain.
Releases resources or declares cleanup complete solely because Future.isDone/isCancelled is true.
Changes to preview structured concurrency or a newer JDK solely to repair this Java 21 fixture.

expectedOutcomes: Read the changed return contract and recognize that per-call close preserves its required no-escape behavior.
Preserve adequate lexical ownership; do not apply the asynchronous-owner redesign merely by preference.
If any refactor is made, prove launch still waits for actual execution completion, including cancellation-insensitive cleanup, rather than just a Future terminal state.
Use a held task to observe no method return before release and a completed result after release.
Retain Java 21 compatibility, exception observation and lifecycle ownership without a performance claim.
controlledChecks: Hold a Callable active and invoke launch on a helper.
After task entry, require the method-return signal to remain absent while execution is deliberately held.
Release the callable; require method return, completed Future/result and no surviving task.
Keep the check bounded and distinguish the contractual no-escape property from a measured latency improvement.
observableFailures: Returns a Future while the controlled task is still active, contradicting the contract.
Demands a long-lived executor or unbounded detached work although lexical waiting is explicitly required.
Treats lack of prompt return as a defect despite the supplied completion-before-return rule.
Claims tests or an independent agent comparison ran when only writing a proposed check.

observedBoundaries: Lexical-return: task active and Future not delivered; after release method returns completed Future.
Timed get expiry plus accepted cancellation: Future done/cancelled while task stays active and caller has not returned.
Interruption of the closing owner does not bypass actual task termination; interrupt status is restored when close returns.
Component owner: Future delivered while task active; later completion/drain succeeds.

The intentionally interrupt-insensitive callable is a controlled lifecycle case, not a claim that every I/O client ignores cancellation.
No real network/client/resource pool, framework shutdown, production deployment, benchmark or broad concurrency proof was executed.
The exact actor fixture only received a trivial smoke execution; the two agent tasks remain pending independent evaluation.
